To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) storytelling in Scratch is a powerful way to introduce middle school students to coding; 2) students' perception of themselves as storytellers is enhanced through coding; and 3) students' perception and use of coding as a tool to create games is enhanced when they are given the opportunity to create interactive games in teams, and 4) the creation of interactive games in Scratch is an effective "hook' to engage students in coding. (Contains 3 tables and 2 figures.)

1) Students' perception of coding is affected by the learning product they create; 2) Students' perception is also affected by their own level of interest and persistence; and 3) Students who are interested and persistent are more likely to have positive perceptions about coding.

students' perception of CS as a practice and their interest and persistence with CS are positively affected by both storytelling and game making in Scratch, and that the latter (game making) is particularly effective in increasing interest in and persistence for CS as a practice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that stories and games play in the introduction of computer science (CS), specifically, the Scratch programming language, to middle school children.
how we can best introduce youth to CS, especially those from traditionally underserved communities.
how we might better engage youth in the practice of computer programming and how we might use the practice to enhance their overall literacy and critical thinking skills. (Author abstract)
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this research shows the importance of storytelling in the introduction of computer science to middle school youth.

the use of storytelling and game creation in the context of a Scratch-based introductory CS course is an effective way to introduce middle school youth to the world of coding, and that the use of these learning "products" (stories and games) can have a significant impact on youth's perception of coding as a practice, their interest in coding, and their overall literacy and computational thinking skills.

the use of Scratch as an introductory CS language in the context of storytelling and game design is a promising approach that can be used to introduce middle school students to the practice of coding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of storytelling and gaming in an introductory CS course is a powerful way to engage youth in coding, particularly when the curriculum is designed to be student-centered and scaffolded in nature.
students' perception of their own ability and interest in CS was enhanced by both story making and game making in Scratch.

the students in our study were able to use the programming language to create a variety of digital stories and games, and that they enjoyed the process and felt empowered to create and control their own stories and games.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the introduction of storytelling and games to the CS classroom is an effective way to introduce youth to the world of coding, and that the introduction of such activities in middle school may be an effective way to lay a foundation for further learning in the subject.

the process of creating stories or games is not the same as the process of learning how to code, and the former may not necessarily be a gateway to the latter, but that the two are not mutually exclusive either.
storytelling and games can serve as effective entry points for youth to learn to code.
